problem: The example calls 'one particle on each side' a macrostate, but the chapter has just defined a macrostate as what is measured on the bench, i.e. U, V, N (and P, T). Under that definition all four arrangements belong to the same macrostate, so calling the one-on-each-side case a macrostate with Ω = 2 contradicts the definition and can confuse a student about what Ω is counting.
fix: Say it explicitly: with only U, V and N fixed, all four microstates are accessible, so Ω = 4 for the macrostate (U, V, N). If a partition or an extra macroscopic constraint fixes one particle on each side, that is a second macrostate, described by the extra variable 'one particle per box', and it has Ω = 2, so kB ln 2 is its entropy.

problem: The phrase 'the macrostate "any arrangement" has Ω = 4' is not a meaningful macrostate label; a macrostate is a set of macroscopic values, not a statement that anything goes.
fix: Write: 'the macrostate fixed by (U, V, N) contains all four microstates, so Ω = 4'.

problem: The wording muddles two different formulas. 'Using R instead of kB gives molar entropy' is only correct when Ω is the number of microstates of one mole; as written a student may conclude S = R ln Ω and S = kB ln Ω are interchangeable for any Ω.
fix: Say: S = kB ln Ω gives the entropy of one system of N particles, with Ω the number of its microstates. For one mole, S = R ln Ω_m, where Ω_m is the number of microstates of the mole and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Match Ω to the amount of substance before choosing kB or R; never mix the two.
